It's just 12 of these popular open-source repos, and then it's only ones where there were tests that passed at the beginning and also new tests that were introduced that test the new feature that's added. So it is, I think, a very limited subset of real engineering tasks, but I think it's also very valuable because even though it's a subset, it is true engineering tasks. A lot of other benchmarks are these much more artificial setups. Even if they're related to coding, they're more like coding interview-style questions or puzzles, which I think are very different from day-to-day. items.question: How do you understand the problem that SWE-bench Verified is trying to fix in the original SWE-bench?
items.object: SWE-bench Verified and the fairness of coding benchmark tasks
items.answer: I think it's 2,000 in the final set, but a lot of those, even though a human did them, are actually impossible given the information that comes with a task. The most classic example is the test looks for a very specific error string, like assert message equals error something something something, and unless you know that's exactly what you're looking for, there's no way the model is going to write that exact same error message, and so the tests are going to fail. SWE-bench Verified was actually made in partnership with OpenAI, and they hired humans to review all these tasks and pick out a subset to try to remove any obstacle like this that would make the tasks impossible. In theory, all of these tasks should be fully doable by the model, and they also had humans grade how difficult they thought the problems would be: less than 15 minutes, 15 minutes to an hour, an hour to four hours, and greater than four hours.

items.question: Why do you favor a minimal agent framework that lets Claude choose its own steps and keep using tools until it thinks it is done?
items.object: Minimal agent frameworks that let Claude choose its own steps and use tools until it considers the task complete
items.answer: A lot of previous agent work built very hardcoded and rigid workflows where the model is pushed through certain flows of steps. To some extent that's needed with smaller models and models that are less smart, but one of the things we really wanted to explore was: let's really give Claude the reins here and not force Claude to do anything, but let Claude decide how it should approach the problem, what steps it should do. The most extreme version of this is just give it some tools that it can call, and it's able to keep calling the tools, keep thinking, and keep doing that until it thinks it's done. That's the most minimal agent framework that we came up with, and I think that works very well. Especially the new Sonnet 3.5 is very good at self-correction. It has a lot of grit. Claude will try things that fail and then come back and try different approaches. That's something you didn't see in a lot of previous models. Some of the existing agent frameworks I looked at had whole systems built to try to detect loops and see, oh, is the model doing the same thing more than three times? Then we have to pull it out. The smarter the models are, the less you need that kind of extra scaffolding. Just give the model tools and let it keep sampling and calling tools until it thinks it's done.

items.question: How do you approach designing tools so an AI model can't use them the wrong way?

items.answer: You can have a plug that can fit either way, and that's dangerous, or you can make it asymmetric so it can't fit this way, it has to go like this. items.question: Why are you excited about computer use as a way to implement tool use?
items.object: Computer use as a lower-friction alternative to API integrations
items.answer: I'm really excited, most broadly, not just for new things that weren't possible before, but as a much lower-friction way to implement tool use. One anecdote from my days at Cobalt Robotics: we wanted our robots to be able to ride elevators to go between floors and fully cover a building. The first way we did this was doing API integrations with the elevator companies. Some of them actually had APIs. We could send a request and it would move the elevator. Each new company we did took like six months because they were very slow and didn't really care about an elevator. Even installing one, once we had it with the company, they would have to literally go install an API box on the elevator that we wanted to use, and that would sometimes take six months. Very slow. Eventually we're like, okay, this is slowing down all of our customer deployments. What if we just add an arm to the robot? I added this little arm that could literally go and press the elevator buttons, and we used computer vision to do this. We could deploy that in a single day and have the robot able to use the elevators. At the same time, it was slower than the API and not quite as reliable. Sometimes it would miss and have to try to press it again, but it would get there. I see this as an analogy to computer use: anything you can do with a computer today, you could probably write tool use and integrate APIs up to the language model, but that's going to take a bunch of software engineering to write those integrations. With computer use, just give the thing a browser that's logged into what you want to integrate with and it's going to work immediately. I see that reduction in friction as incredibly exciting. Imagine a customer support team where you have a customer support bot, but you need to integrate it with all these things, and you don't have any engineers on your customer support team. If you can just give the thing a browser that's logged into your systems that you need it to have access to, suddenly in one day you could be up and rolling with a fully integrated customer service bot.

items.question: Why do you see general-purpose language models as a major unlock for robotics?
items.object: General-purpose language models as an unlock for robotics
items.answer: So take everything with a grain of salt. I'll start with the positives. There is incredible progress that's happened in the last five years that I think will be a big unlock for robotics. The first is general-purpose language models. There was an old saying in robotics that if fully describing your task is harder than just doing the task, you can never automate it, because it's going to take more effort to tell the robot how to do this thing than to just do it yourself. LLMs solved that. I no longer need to exhaustively program in every little thing. The thing has common sense. It's going to know, how do I make a Reuben sandwich? I'm not going to have to program that in. Before, even a cooking thing would be, oh God, we're going to have a team of engineers hard-coding recipes for the long tail of anything. It'd be a disaster. Bringing common sense really solves this huge problem of describing tasks.

items.question: How do you assess the promise of diffusion-inspired path planning for robotics?
items.object: Diffusion-inspired path planning and generalization in robotics
items.answer: The second big innovation has been diffusion models for path planning. A lot of this work came out of Toyota Research. There are a lot of startups working on this, like Physical Intelligence, PI, Chelsea Finn's startup at Stanford. The basic idea is using a bit more inspiration from diffusion rather than diffusion models themselves, but they are a way to basically learn an end-to-end motion control. Previously all robotics motion control was hardcoded: you were programming explicit motions or programming an explicit goal and using an optimization library to find the shortest path to it. This is now something where you give it a bunch of demonstrations and, just like deep learning, it's learning from these examples what it means to go pick up a cup. In a way, just like diffusion models, they are somewhat conditioned by text. You can have the same model learn many different tasks, and the hope is that these start to generalize: if you've trained it on picking up coffee cups and picking up books, then when I say pick up the backpack, it knows how to do that even though you've never trained it on that. That's the Holy Grail here: train it on 500 different tasks and that's enough to really get it to generalize to do anything you would need. I think that's still a big TBD. These people have measured some degree of generalization, but at the end of the day, like LLMs, do you really care about the thing being able to do something that no one has ever shown in training data? For a home robot, there are a hundred things people really want to do, and you can make sure it has good training for those things. What you do care about is generalization within a task: I've never seen this particular coffee mug before; can I still pick it up? The models do seem very good at that.

items.question: Why do you see reliability as the main obstacle to making robots useful in homes and factories?

items.answer: For robotics, I think the limiting factor is going to be reliability. These models are really good at doing demos of doing laundry or dishes. If they only work 99% of the time, that sounds good, but it's actually really annoying. Humans are really good at these tasks. Imagine if one out of every 100 dishes it washed, it breaks. You would not want that robot in your house, or in your factory if one of every hundred boxes it moves it drops and breaks things inside. For these things to really be useful, they're going to have to hit a very high level of reliability, just like self-driving cars. items.question: What do you see as the central difficulty in building reliable robot hardware at scale?
items.object: Building reliable robot hardware at scale
items.answer: Hardware is just so hard. You build your first robot and it works; you're like, great. Then you build 10 of them: five work, three work half the time, two of them don't work, and you built them all the same and you don't know why. The real world has this level of detail and differences that software doesn't have. Imagine if every for-loop you wrote, some of them just didn't work, some of them were slower than others. How do you deal with that? Imagine if every binary you shipped to a customer, each of those for-loops was a little different. It becomes so hard to scale and maintain quality of these things. That's what makes hardware really hard: not building one of something, but repeatedly building something and making it work reliably. You'll buy a batch of 100 motors and each of those motors will behave a little bit differently to the same input command. My lived experience at Cobalt Robotics was all about how you build something robust despite these differences. We can't get the tolerance of motors down. It's everything.

items.question: What did debugging thermal-camera failures on your robots teach you about hardware reliability?

items.answer: At a certain point, a bunch of these thermal cameras started failing, and we couldn't figure out why. I asked everyone on the team, hey, what's changed? Did the software change around this? No. Did the hardware design change? No. I was investigating all this stuff, looking at kernel logs, and finally the procurement person was like, oh yeah, I found this new vendor for USB cables last summer. I was like, what, you switched which vendor we're buying USB cables from? It's the same exact cable, just a dollar cheaper. It turns out that was the problem: this new cable had slightly worse resistance or slightly worse EMI interference, and it worked most of the time, but 1% of the time these cameras would fail and we'd need to reboot a big part of the system. It was all because these two different USB cables had the same exact spec but were slightly different. These are the kinds of things you deal with with hardware.
